purpose: Audit varied public NHS website templates and an anonymous navigation route to general walking information; exclude diagnosis, accounts, booking and personal health submissions.

protocol.states: Initial desktop, then same document resized to 360 CSS px, live reduced-motion and dark changes, print emulation, twelve Tab presses; separate fresh no-JavaScript and dark contexts. Resized and emulated states are not independent cold loads or real-device tests.
protocol.measurementPurpose: Qualitative review and bounded interaction evidence, not headline bytes or energy
limitations: Main document observations; embedded frames are not traversed
Page probes include bounded Tab traversal after other states; no control activation. Journey actions must be explicit
Selected CDP response headers omit cookies and authorization; no header alone proves cache reuse
Keyboard trace is twelve Tab presses, not complete keyboard or accessibility conformance
Resource Timing zeros may reflect timing restrictions or cache, not zero traffic
Notification requestPermission calls counted with a delegating wrapper
Print emulation is not PDF pagination or document accessibility testing

checkDefinitions.expectation: Assess visible distractions against the declared visitor task; distinguish useful prompts from interruptions.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Inspect choice wording, defaults, prominence and the observed accept/reject paths for undue steering. DOM text alone does not establish visual parity.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Assess the sampled task's wording, headings and terminology for its stated audience; retain uncertainty about unrepresented users.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Compare repeated navigation and control names across sampled pages; consistent samples do not prove a documented design system.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Assess observed animation purpose, playback controls and reduced-motion behavior. A quiet snapshot does not prove no motion occurs elsewhere.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Assess observed alerts and notification permission requests for user value and choice; absence is limited to observed states.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Review print layout visibility and download labels for the declared task. Fetch and inspect document content before asserting optimization or equivalence.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Use initial JS/CSS execution observations to nominate investigation targets; require representative journeys or source corroboration before recommending removal.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Relate initial script resources to visible components and later task needs; recommend splitting only when a component's deferred use and usable activation are corroborated.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Compare narrow and desktop task content and overflow, then exercise affected controls; width emulation alone is not real-device compatibility.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Identify consequential user choices in the sample and assess whether contextual impact information is useful and supported. Do not prescribe carbon labels on every control.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Execute declared task actions and inspect completion evidence; an expected selector is one observable, not proof of user success or optimal journey length.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Cite page/state or journey JSON Pointers, declared task and sample. Use additional screenshots, task observations, document content or source when the expectation cannot be resolved from the collected facts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled task images preserve useful content and provide proportionate intrinsic dimensions and delivery choices for their rendered size and pixel density. A large image is an investigation candidate until legibility and task value are checked; absent srcset alone is not a failure.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Compare desktop/narrow image dimensions, srcset/sizes, delivered MIME types, loading state, and task content. Confirm any proposed rendition at intended pixel densities before asserting savings.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Observed web fonts and variants serve the sampled content, with a declared fallback/loading strategy where needed. Do not fail a site merely for using a web font; recommend removal or subsetting only after language and readability requirements are established.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Inspect document.fonts family/weight/style/display/status, font responses and visible body text. Missing font-blocking/constrained-loading or language evidence can leave the scoped judgment unresolved.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled document has a meaningful language, primary heading and main region, and task controls have visible labels or an explicit naming relationship. Count/attribute presence alone does not establish semantic correctness or WCAG compliance.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Read title/lang/headings/mainCount, form control labels and task content. aria-labelledby references need resolution before claiming a missing accessible name.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled content has a descriptive title and usable canonical metadata when applicable; declared structured-data blocks parse as JSON. Judge description and other optional metadata according to page purpose, not a mandatory-field checklist.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Inspect metadata and document title, resolving canonical URLs and applicability. JSON parsing does not establish schema validity or search-engine eligibility.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled page respects applicable dark/reduced-motion preferences both before navigation and when they change in-page, without losing task content. Distinguish intentional design choices and absence of applicable motion from unsupported behavior.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Compare desktop, reduced_motion, live_dark and cold_dark observations, colors, visible text and actual animations. A matching media query alone is insufficient; theme initialization and live change are distinct.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled core reading content and navigation remain available without JavaScript, or an explicit alternative supports the task. This bounded check does not establish no-JavaScript search, every interaction, or all browser compatibility.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Compare desktop and fresh no_javascript text/headings/navigation. Explain task-critical missing content and legitimate progressive enhancements rather than demanding every feature without scripts.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Repeated observed API requests are justified by the sampled task and its update needs. Identify redundant-looking requests for investigation without inferring backend cost or safe removal from URL repetition alone.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Inspect bounded network.requests methods/types/timestamps and explicit journey resource entries. Establish polling purpose, cache behavior and task freshness needs; initial-only windows may remain cantTell.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Reusable public scripts/styles/media expose an appropriate caching or validation policy in the sample. Distinguish dynamic/private responses and note that headers alone do not prove cache reuse or offline support.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Review allowlisted response cache-control/etag/last-modified/age/vary headers and public resource purpose. Require a warm-load test before claiming measured reuse; private no-store is a legitimate exception.

checkDefinitions.expectation: Material sampled text assets are delivered with compression where beneficial. Do not demand compression for already-compressed images, tiny bodies or error responses without context.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Review text/script/style response MIME types, status and content-encoding, alongside transfer magnitude when available. Header absence for a material text response supports investigation; missing response evidence stays unknown.

checkDefinitions.expectation: The sampled initial keyboard path reaches visible task navigation/controls in a meaningful order with a discernible focus indicator. A bounded Tab trace cannot establish complete keyboard support, reverse navigation, traps or screen-reader accessibility.
checkDefinitions.evidenceRequirements: Inspect keyboardFocus steps, names/label relationships, element geometry, focus-visible and outline clues. A zero outline is not proof of invisible focus because borders or shadows may supply it; verify the actual indicator before a failure.

Walking for health

Walking is simple, free and one of the easiest ways to get more active, lose weight and become healthier.

Sometimes overlooked as a form of exercise, walking briskly can help you build stamina, burn excess calories and make your heart healthier.

You do not have to walk for hours. A brisk 10-minute daily walk has lots of health benefits and counts towards your 150 minutes of weekly exercise, as recommended in the physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64.

Walking for health

Walking is simple, free and one of the easiest ways to get more active, lose weight and become healthier.

Sometimes overlooked as a form of exercise, walking briskly can help you build stamina, burn excess calories and make your heart healthier.

You do not have to walk for hours. A brisk 10-minute daily walk has lots of health benefits and counts towards your 150 minutes of weekly exercise, as recommended in the physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64.

Before you start

Any shoes or trainers that are comfortable, provide adequate support and do not cause blisters will do.

If you're walking to work, you could wear your usual work clothes with a comfy pair of shoes and change shoes when you get into work.

For long walks, you may want to take some water, healthy snacks, a spare top, sunscreen and a sun hat in a small backpack.

If you start going for longer walks regularly, you may want to invest in a waterproof jacket and some specialist walking shoes for more challenging routes.

How do I know if I'm walking fast enough?

A brisk walk is about 3 miles an hour, which is faster than a stroll.

You can tell you're walking briskly if you can still talk but cannot sing the words to a song.

You could also try using the free Active 10 app on your smartphone.

It tells you when you're walking fast enough and suggests ways to fit in some more brisk walking.

Download Active 10 from the NHS Better Health website

What if I'm not very active?

If you're not very active but are able to walk, increase your walking distance gradually.

If your joints are a problem, check whether your local swimming pool holds exercise classes.

The water helps to support your joints while you move and can help you strengthen your muscles.

If you cannot leave the house, why not see if one of our free Fitness Studio exercise videos can help.

Staying motivated
Make it a habit

The easiest way to walk more is to make walking a habit.

Think of ways to include walking in your daily routine.

Examples include: 

walking part of your journey to work
walking to the shops
using the stairs instead of the lift
leaving the car behind for short journeys
walking the kids to school
doing a regular walk with a friend
going for a stroll with family or friends after dinner

Walking while listening to music or a podcast can take your mind off the effort.

It can also get you into a rhythm and help you walk faster.

You'll be surprised at how fast the time goes when you're walking to your favourite tunes.

Content policy

The NHS website is committed to the highest editorial and ethical standards in the provision of all its content and related services.

The site is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. The content, data and services on the NHS website are commissioned by NHS England and delivered by NHS Digital.

The NHS website is committed to providing objective and trustworthy information and guidance on all aspects of health and healthcare.

The overall NHS website content policy covers all content, both data-driven – directories and comparative data – and editorial. The latter includes written content, video and audio resources, interactive tools and images.

In all instances, we strive to ensure that data is accurate and clearly presented and that editorial content meets users' needs, is clinically safe and evidence-based – in other words, that it is founded on the best scientific knowledge and research currently available.

All clinical content on the NHS website is checked and approved by an appropriately qualified and experienced member of our internal clinical team. For specialist content, we may consult practising doctors or other external subject matter experts.

The following sections set out our editorial principles, standards and processes.

Principles
Accuracy

Content on the NHS website will be accurate, balanced and transparent. Information given will be based on the best available scientific evidence and data sources. Where content contains conjecture or opinion, this will be clearly indicated.

Impartiality and diversity of opinion

The NHS website will be objective, impartial and even-handed. Where views differ and no scientific consensus can be found it will reflect all significant strands of opinion and state the uncertainty clearly.

Accountability

The NHS website is accountable to its users and will deal fairly with them. It will be open in admitting mistakes and encourages a culture of learning through user feedback. Its editorial processes will be transparent.

Serving the public

The NHS website will put its users' interests first when sourcing and developing content. It will consult widely with relevant professional bodies, patient organisations, charities and other interest groups but meeting users' needs will remain paramount.

Taste and decency

All content on the NHS website will be suitable for a general audience and will not include material that might reasonably be deemed offensive. Where content includes explicit sexual information it will be clearly flagged.

Privacy

The NHS website views its users' privacy as paramount. Find out more about privacy on the NHS website.

Funding

The NHS website is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. It does not carry advertising and does not accept corporate sponsorship.

Standards
Staff interests and independence

The NHS website has a dedicated content team. It has a clear mandate to produce accurate, balanced and transparent information that meets the needs of users.

No member of staff will be asked, or is permitted, to provide favoured treatment to any partner organisation, and all staff must fully disclose any financial or other interests they may have in any healthcare-related companies or organisations. Such interests must be reported to the site's Content Director at the time of employment or at the point the interests arise thereafter.

The Content Director will report any potential conflict of interest to the Programme's Director and the Programme's Clinical Lead who will determine what needs to be done to eliminate it. Where content is produced by outside organisations or individuals, NHS.UK requires that such agents make a similar disclosure of outside interests.

Training

All content team members are given training to ensure editorial standards are met. Specifically, they are trained to search for and review high-quality evidence to make sure that content is factually and clinically accurate.

Quality assurance

The Programme's Clinical Lead, reporting to NHS Digital's Chief Medical Officers, is accountable for making sure the content we publish has a clear evidence base, is clinically safe, meets users' needs and supports the NHS.

The Content Director is accountable for the maintenance of general editorial standards, in particular for making sure that content meets the Standard for creating health content (in the NHS digital service manual).

Editorial process
Research

The evidence-based knowledge that informs all NHS.UK content is derived from:

user research with patients and the public
the most authoritative clinical sources
direct experience of clinicians and other health professionals

In pulling together this knowledge to provide users with a rounded and balanced package of material on a particular subject, the NHS website requires its staff and contractors to consult the following resources.

For peer-reviewed scientific research, they consult reputable sources of clinical evidence, such as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS).

Where knowledge of direct experience is required, they consult:

patients and members of the public who may be affected by a topic or issue
practising doctors and other clinicians with direct and current experience in dealing with or treating the health issue under investigation
medical royal colleges
national charities with a recognised expertise and specialist interest
patient organisations

Resources used in the development of content are available on request. You can contact the NHS website team.

Production

New content or major changes are checked by a senior and experienced member of staff. They are checked for:

accuracy
balance
accessibility
tone
Clinical sign-off

Before any content containing clinical information is published on the NHS website, 1 or more clinicians must confirm that it is accurate, clinically safe and reflects relevant evidence.

Content types and clinical approval
Type of content	Approved by


All clinical information

	

A member of the internal (NHS Digital) clinical team




New content, major changes, videos and images

	

2 members of the internal clinical team




Content about public health emergencies or fast-changing public health policy where the internal clinical team identifies a potential clinical, system-wide or reputational impact

	

NHS Digital's Chief Medical Officer or someone they delegate to

Content may also be read and approved by other appropriately qualified and experienced clinicians (and the internal clinical team may require that it is) but final clinical sign-off is provided by the internal clinical team.

Policy sign-off

Prior to publication, if there is a relevant policy, content must also be read by an appropriate policy official, either at the Department of Health and Social Care or NHS England, who checks it for alignment with that policy.

Final editorial checks

Final content is then checked for:

common factual errors
spelling
grammar
adherence to house style
Review of content

Editorial content on the NHS website is reviewed systematically. All editorial content is reviewed at least every 3 years.

Evidence updates to published content, as well as feedback from users and stakeholders, are considered on a day-by-day basis as they arrive, and content is reviewed and amended immediately if necessary.

Publication dates are displayed on all content.

Social media policy

All content made for the NHS website social media channels (Twitter, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook) follows the processes for clinical sign-off and editorial checks described in this policy.

Videos shared on our YouTube channel are reviewed at least every 3 years.

Health information that does not reflect current evidence is suspended and is not available to view. It will be updated, replaced, or removed.

We do not review or remove historic content posted to Twitter, Instagram or Facebook. The content is accurate when we publish it online. The date of publication is shown alongside any posts on the social media channels we use.

New content in development

We are developing various new content products that are tested with the public before they go live. We signpost to users that these are prototypes and not final products. Not all the provisions of this policy apply to content in development.

Feedback and complaints about the NHS website

The NHS website welcomes feedback on all its content. You can contact the NHS website team.

Your feedback or complaint will be sent to our Service Desk team. The team will pass it to the appropriate content team member or clinician. Alternatively, you can email us at nhswebsite.servicedesk@nhs.net.

In the event that a complaint cannot be resolved by a member of the team responsible for the NHS website, it will be escalated under NHS Digital's complaints procedure.

Content policy

The NHS website is committed to the highest editorial and ethical standards in the provision of all its content and related services.

The site is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. The content, data and services on the NHS website are commissioned by NHS England and delivered by NHS Digital.

The NHS website is committed to providing objective and trustworthy information and guidance on all aspects of health and healthcare.

The overall NHS website content policy covers all content, both data-driven – directories and comparative data – and editorial. The latter includes written content, video and audio resources, interactive tools and images.

In all instances, we strive to ensure that data is accurate and clearly presented and that editorial content meets users' needs, is clinically safe and evidence-based – in other words, that it is founded on the best scientific knowledge and research currently available.

All clinical content on the NHS website is checked and approved by an appropriately qualified and experienced member of our internal clinical team. For specialist content, we may consult practising doctors or other external subject matter experts.

The following sections set out our editorial principles, standards and processes.

Principles
Accuracy

Content on the NHS website will be accurate, balanced and transparent. Information given will be based on the best available scientific evidence and data sources. Where content contains conjecture or opinion, this will be clearly indicated.

Impartiality and diversity of opinion

The NHS website will be objective, impartial and even-handed. Where views differ and no scientific consensus can be found it will reflect all significant strands of opinion and state the uncertainty clearly.

Accountability

The NHS website is accountable to its users and will deal fairly with them. It will be open in admitting mistakes and encourages a culture of learning through user feedback. Its editorial processes will be transparent.

Serving the public

The NHS website will put its users' interests first when sourcing and developing content. It will consult widely with relevant professional bodies, patient organisations, charities and other interest groups but meeting users' needs will remain paramount.

Taste and decency

All content on the NHS website will be suitable for a general audience and will not include material that might reasonably be deemed offensive. Where content includes explicit sexual information it will be clearly flagged.

Privacy

The NHS website views its users' privacy as paramount. Find out more about privacy on the NHS website.

Funding

The NHS website is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. It does not carry advertising and does not accept corporate sponsorship.

Standards
Staff interests and independence

The NHS website has a dedicated content team. It has a clear mandate to produce accurate, balanced and transparent information that meets the needs of users.

No member of staff will be asked, or is permitted, to provide favoured treatment to any partner organisation, and all staff must fully disclose any financial or other interests they may have in any healthcare-related companies or organisations. Such interests must be reported to the site's Content Director at the time of employment or at the point the interests arise thereafter.

The Content Director will report any potential conflict of interest to the Programme's Director and the Programme's Clinical Lead who will determine what needs to be done to eliminate it. Where content is produced by outside organisations or individuals, NHS.UK requires that such agents make a similar disclosure of outside interests.

Training

All content team members are given training to ensure editorial standards are met. Specifically, they are trained to search for and review high-quality evidence to make sure that content is factually and clinically accurate.

Quality assurance

The Programme's Clinical Lead, reporting to NHS Digital's Chief Medical Officers, is accountable for making sure the content we publish has a clear evidence base, is clinically safe, meets users' needs and supports the NHS.

The Content Director is accountable for the maintenance of general editorial standards, in particular for making sure that content meets the Standard for creating health content (in the NHS digital service manual).

Editorial process
Research

The evidence-based knowledge that informs all NHS.UK content is derived from:

user research with patients and the public
the most authoritative clinical sources
direct experience of clinicians and other health professionals

In pulling together this knowledge to provide users with a rounded and balanced package of material on a particular subject, the NHS website requires its staff and contractors to consult the following resources.

For peer-reviewed scientific research, they consult reputable sources of clinical evidence, such as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS).

Where knowledge of direct experience is required, they consult:

patients and members of the public who may be affected by a topic or issue
practising doctors and other clinicians with direct and current experience in dealing with or treating the health issue under investigation
medical royal colleges
national charities with a recognised expertise and specialist interest
patient organisations

Resources used in the development of content are available on request. You can contact the NHS website team.

Production

New content or major changes are checked by a senior and experienced member of staff. They are checked for:

accuracy
balance
accessibility
tone
Clinical sign-off

Before any content containing clinical information is published on the NHS website, 1 or more clinicians must confirm that it is accurate, clinically safe and reflects relevant evidence.

Content types and clinical approval
Type of content	Approved by


All clinical information

	

A member of the internal (NHS Digital) clinical team




New content, major changes, videos and images

	

2 members of the internal clinical team




Content about public health emergencies or fast-changing public health policy where the internal clinical team identifies a potential clinical, system-wide or reputational impact

	

NHS Digital's Chief Medical Officer or someone they delegate to

Content may also be read and approved by other appropriately qualified and experienced clinicians (and the internal clinical team may require that it is) but final clinical sign-off is provided by the internal clinical team.

Policy sign-off

Prior to publication, if there is a relevant policy, content must also be read by an appropriate policy official, either at the Department of Health and Social Care or NHS England, who checks it for alignment with that policy.

Final editorial checks

Final content is then checked for:

common factual errors
spelling
grammar
adherence to house style
Review of content

Editorial content on the NHS website is reviewed systematically. All editorial content is reviewed at least every 3 years.

Evidence updates to published content, as well as feedback from users and stakeholders, are considered on a day-by-day basis as they arrive, and content is reviewed and amended immediately if necessary.

Publication dates are displayed on all content.

Social media policy

All content made for the NHS website social media channels (Twitter, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook) follows the processes for clinical sign-off and editorial checks described in this policy.

Videos shared on our YouTube channel are reviewed at least every 3 years.

Health information that does not reflect current evidence is suspended and is not available to view. It will be updated, replaced, or removed.

We do not review or remove historic content posted to Twitter, Instagram or Facebook. The content is accurate when we publish it online. The date of publication is shown alongside any posts on the social media channels we use.

New content in development

We are developing various new content products that are tested with the public before they go live. We signpost to users that these are prototypes and not final products. Not all the provisions of this policy apply to content in development.

Feedback and complaints about the NHS website

The NHS website welcomes feedback on all its content. You can contact the NHS website team.

Your feedback or complaint will be sent to our Service Desk team. The team will pass it to the appropriate content team member or clinician. Alternatively, you can email us at nhswebsite.servicedesk@nhs.net.

In the event that a complaint cannot be resolved by a member of the team responsible for the NHS website, it will be escalated under NHS Digital's complaints procedure.

Content policy

The NHS website is committed to the highest editorial and ethical standards in the provision of all its content and related services.

The site is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. The content, data and services on the NHS website are commissioned by NHS England and delivered by NHS Digital.

The NHS website is committed to providing objective and trustworthy information and guidance on all aspects of health and healthcare.

The overall NHS website content policy covers all content, both data-driven – directories and comparative data – and editorial. The latter includes written content, video and audio resources, interactive tools and images.

In all instances, we strive to ensure that data is accurate and clearly presented and that editorial content meets users' needs, is clinically safe and evidence-based – in other words, that it is founded on the best scientific knowledge and research currently available.

All clinical content on the NHS website is checked and approved by an appropriately qualified and experienced member of our internal clinical team. For specialist content, we may consult practising doctors or other external subject matter experts.

The following sections set out our editorial principles, standards and processes.

Principles
Accuracy

Content on the NHS website will be accurate, balanced and transparent. Information given will be based on the best available scientific evidence and data sources. Where content contains conjecture or opinion, this will be clearly indicated.

Impartiality and diversity of opinion

The NHS website will be objective, impartial and even-handed. Where views differ and no scientific consensus can be found it will reflect all significant strands of opinion and state the uncertainty clearly.

Accountability

The NHS website is accountable to its users and will deal fairly with them. It will be open in admitting mistakes and encourages a culture of learning through user feedback. Its editorial processes will be transparent.

Serving the public

The NHS website will put its users' interests first when sourcing and developing content. It will consult widely with relevant professional bodies, patient organisations, charities and other interest groups but meeting users' needs will remain paramount.

Taste and decency

All content on the NHS website will be suitable for a general audience and will not include material that might reasonably be deemed offensive. Where content includes explicit sexual information it will be clearly flagged.

Privacy

The NHS website views its users' privacy as paramount. Find out more about privacy on the NHS website.

Funding

The NHS website is funded by the Department of Health and Social Care. It does not carry advertising and does not accept corporate sponsorship.

Standards
Staff interests and independence

The NHS website has a dedicated content team. It has a clear mandate to produce accurate, balanced and transparent information that meets the needs of users.

No member of staff will be asked, or is permitted, to provide favoured treatment to any partner organisation, and all staff must fully disclose any financial or other interests they may have in any healthcare-related companies or organisations. Such interests must be reported to the site's Content Director at the time of employment or at the point the interests arise thereafter.

The Content Director will report any potential conflict of interest to the Programme's Director and the Programme's Clinical Lead who will determine what needs to be done to eliminate it. Where content is produced by outside organisations or individuals, NHS.UK requires that such agents make a similar disclosure of outside interests.

Training

All content team members are given training to ensure editorial standards are met. Specifically, they are trained to search for and review high-quality evidence to make sure that content is factually and clinically accurate.

The Content Director is accountable for the maintenance of general editorial standards, in particular for making sure that content meets the Standard for creating health content (in the NHS digital service manual).

Research

The evidence-based knowledge that informs all NHS.UK content is derived from:

user research with patients and the public
the most authoritative clinical sources
direct experience of clinicians and other health professionals

For peer-reviewed scientific research, they consult reputable sources of clinical evidence, such as the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS).

Where knowledge of direct experience is required, they consult:

patients and members of the public who may be affected by a topic or issue
practising doctors and other clinicians with direct and current experience in dealing with or treating the health issue under investigation
medical royal colleges
national charities with a recognised expertise and specialist interest
patient organisations

Healthy living
Exercise
Walking for health

Walking is simple, free and one of the easiest ways to get more active, lose weight and become healthier.

Sometimes overlooked as a form of exercise, walking briskly can help you build stamina, burn excess calories and make your heart healthier.

You do not have to walk for hours. A brisk 10-minute daily walk has lots of health benefits and counts towards your 150 minutes of weekly exercise, as recommended in the physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64.

Before you start

Any shoes or trainers that are comfortable, provide adequate support and do not cause blisters will do.

If you're walking to work, you could wear your usual work clothes with a comfy pair of shoes and change shoes when you get into work.

For long walks, you may want to take some water, healthy snacks, a spare top, sunscreen and a sun hat in a small backpack.

If you start going for longer walks regularly, you may want to invest in a waterproof jacket and some specialist walking shoes for more challenging routes.

How do I know if I'm walking fast enough?

A brisk walk is about 3 miles an hour, which is faster than a stroll.

You can tell you're walking briskly if you can still talk but cannot sing the words to a song.

You could also try using the free Active 10 app on your smartphone.

It tells you when you're walking fast enough and suggests ways to fit in some more brisk walking.

Download Active 10 from the NHS Better Health website

What if I'm not very active?

If you're not very active but are able to walk, increase your walking distance gradually.

If your joints are a problem, check whether your local swimming pool holds exercise classes.

The water helps to support your joints while you move and can help you strengthen your muscles.

If you cannot leave the house, why not see if one of our free Fitness Studio exercise videos can help.

Staying motivated
Make it a habit

The easiest way to walk more is to make walking a habit.

Think of ways to include walking in your daily routine.

Examples include: 

walking part of your journey to work
walking to the shops
using the stairs instead of the lift
leaving the car behind for short journeys
walking the kids to school
doing a regular walk with a friend
going for a stroll with family or friends after dinner
Listen to music

Walking while listening to music or a podcast can take your mind off the effort.

It can also get you into a rhythm and help you walk faster.

You'll be surprised at how fast the time goes when you're walking to your favourite tunes.

Use the Active 10 app

Active 10 allows you to track how much and how fast you have walked. 

To keep things interesting, it gives you goals to work towards and rewards your progress.

Download Active 10 from the NHS Better Health website

Mix it up

Add variety to your walks. You do not have to travel to the countryside to find a rewarding walk.

Towns and cities offer interesting walks, including parks, heritage trails, canal towpaths, riverside paths, commons, woodlands, heaths and nature reserves.

Join a walking group

Walking in a group is a great way to start walking, make new friends and stay motivated.

Ramblers organises group walks for health, leisure and as a means of getting around for people of all ages, backgrounds and levels of fitness.

For details of many locally organised walks in towns and cities, as well as the countryside, visit the Ramblers website.
